# Generate Turing or PracticalBayes code

[`turing_code`](@ref) writes the model that `brm` fits as a Turing.jl
`@model`, the way brms's `stancode` writes Stan code. Use it to see exactly
what a formula means, or as a starting point for a model that brms syntax
cannot express. [`pb_code`](@ref) does the same for PracticalBayes.jl.

```julia
using PracticalBayesianRegression

f = @bf(y ~ x + (1 | g))
code = turing_code(f, df; family = poisson())
```

```
using Turing, LinearAlgebra
# Generated by PracticalBayesianRegression.turing_code.
# formula: y~x+(1|g)
# family:  poisson (log link)
# Data: `model_data(...)` returns the arguments in order.
@model function regression_model(y, X, means_X, J_g, N_g)
    # population-level effects (X is centred; Intercept is the centred intercept, as in brms)
    Intercept ~ 2.5 * TDist(3)
    b ~ filldist(Flat(), 1)
    b_Intercept := Intercept - dot(means_X, b)
    # group-level effects (Intercept | g), non-centred as in brms
    sd_g ~ truncated(2.5 * TDist(3); lower=0)
    z_g ~ filldist(Normal(), N_g)
    r_g = sd_g .* z_g
    eta = Intercept .+ X * b .+ r_g[J_g]
    # likelihood
    y ~ arraydist(LogPoisson.(eta))
end
```

The code uses the same design matrices, centring, parameterisation and
default priors as `brm`. [`model_data`](@ref) returns the arguments it takes.
`turing_code(fit)` writes the code for a fitted model.

## Edit and run it

Save the code, change it, and run it with Turing:

```julia
write("model.jl", code)
# ... edit model.jl ...
using Turing
include("model.jl")
m = regression_model(model_data(f, df; family = poisson())...)
chain = sample(m, NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), 1000, 4)
```

To run the generated model unchanged, [`turing_model`](@ref) evaluates the
code and applies it to the data in one step (and [`pb_model`](@ref) for
PracticalBayes):

```julia
using Turing
m = turing_model(f, df; family = poisson())
chain = sample(m, NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), 1000, 4)
```

`turing_model` defines the model function when it is called. Inside a
function, sample through `Base.invokelatest(sample, m, NUTS(), 1000)`.

## Speed

The generated model is evaluated by Turing (or PracticalBayes) with automatic
differentiation, not by this package's closed-form gradient, so it is not
guaranteed to be as fast as `brm`, and is usually slower.

## Models the generator cannot write out

Every model gets code, but not every feature can be written out explicitly
yet. For those models the code samples the unconstrained parameter vector
and adds the package's own log density with
[`model_logdensity`](@ref). The posterior is the same; the code is just less
readable. `code.fallback` names the feature responsible:

```julia
code = turing_code(fit)
code.fallback          # "" when the code is explicit
turing_code(fit; fallback = false)   # raise an error instead
```

Families without a Distributions.jl equivalent appear as
[`FamilyDist`](@ref), the package's own distribution type for them.
